latest_comment.raw_content:
Dear fellow investors,

Over the past twelve months, 𝗺𝘆 𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝟮𝟮%, 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦&𝗣 𝟱𝟬𝟬 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝟭𝟰% in the same period.

The best performing stocks in the past twelve months for me have been $MU and $SMSN.L.

The worst performers have been $AVAV and $1810.HK. AeroVironment lost a major contract and continues to make next to no profits, despite having grown the business significantly. Xiaomi's profit levels have declined significantly, including from lower phone sales and higher memory chip costs.

For $MU and $SMSN.L, the key success factor is the 𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀. In a data centre there are three main types of memory. You can think of them like the short-term, medium-term and long-term memory.

High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is the fastest version of the medium-term memory. AI is pushing the need for all the types of memory, but this one in particular, as that is how you store the vast array of numbers that is the core of the AI. 

The short-term memory is too small to hold that data at once and the long-term memory too slow to give you a quick result.

This is ultimately why the boom in 𝗔𝗜 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘄𝗶𝗱𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 (𝗛𝗕𝗠) 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿. And when you see the latest and future roadmap of the data centre builders, you see that the key performance metrics are highly driven by the amount of HBM chips they’ve managed to get into their designs. 

Many older investors have been wary of investing into the memory chip manufacturers though. 

They remember the times when 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘂𝗺 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗻𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀 over short periods of time, as the 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝘂𝗽 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆.

In an industry with multiple manufacturers, when the market is good, it can be clear to them all that there is an opportunity for one more factory. But if they each build a new factory, that may be too many. So who shall go ahead and build one? They would each like to be the one to build one, but only if the others don’t. This is a tricky competitive situation – where you must analyse your competitors very carefully and manage your own communications and signalling carefully. Ideally you can build a factory, and influence others into not building more factories. 

Thankfully, today in the HBM business, there are just three manufacturers, and a need for a lot more factories (or mostly higher production output from existing factories that can be expanded and improved). 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗴𝗼 𝗮𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘅𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻. Customers are willing to pre-pay to receive their chips years in the future.

While it is difficult this time for the manufacturers to massively ramp up capacity like in previous cycles, the excess demand could disappear. China has plans within HBM as well – so it should be expected that long term, there will be a stronger fourth manufacturer in China. 

If further AI development is banned, if AI capabilities do not improve sufficiently, if energy or construction bottlenecks prevent the building of more data centres, or other bottlenecks e.g. from 𝗮 𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗧𝗮𝗶𝘄𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗼𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘀 – 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘀𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝘂𝗿𝘁 𝗛𝗕𝗠 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱.

A good portfolio should be built to do well in many potential future scenarios, not just in the most likely one. But it doesn’t hurt to be positioned to do very well in the most likely future scenario. 

You can rest assured that I will stay on top of the developments - every day.

Best regards,
Jeppe Kirk Bonde
